tone_statements.citation: Kari, Ethelbert Emmanuel. 2019. The languages of Rivers State of Nigeria: An overview. Marang: Journal of Language and Literature 31: 1-22. Gaborone: University of Botswana. ISSN 1816-7659.
tone_statements.quote: Tone is another interesting phonological characteristic of Rivers State languages. In all Rivers State languages, the pitch of the voice can be used to distinguish words, phrases and sentences whose segmental compositions are otherwise the same. [...] The tones that are attested in Rivers State languages include high (́), mid (ˉ), low (̀), and downstepped-high tone (a phonetically lowered high tone in the environment of a preceding floating low tone represented with an arrow pointing downwards between two high-toned syllables σ́ꜜσ́).
tone_statements.locator: p. 11, sec. 5.1 Phonological Profile of Rivers State Languages

tone_statements.citation: Kari, Ethelbert E. 2007. The pronominal system of Oḍual. Studies in African Linguistics 36(1): 91-113. DOI 10.32473/sal.v36i1.107306.
tone_statements.quote: There are two basic tones in Odual, low and high, plus a downstep. In this paper only the high and the downstep are marked. The high tone is marked ( '), while the downstep is marked (6·6) with an arrow pointing downwards between two high-toned moras. In general, the low tone is not marked for the sake of convenience. … Tonally, the first person singular and first person plural exclusive subject pronouns have a high tone pattern, i.e. all moras are high toned; … while the second person singular subject pronoun has a high-downstepped-high tone pattern.
tone_statements.locator: p. 94 footnote 5 and p. 95 sec. 3.1.1 Subject pronouns

sources.note: No phonology; only that Odual differs from Abua in 'intonation, with the Oduals having a more rising intonation'. Works-cited list matches Glottolog plus Kari 2011 orthography and Kari 2007a.

sources.citation: Kari, Ethelbert Emmanuel. 2017. Central Delta languages: An overview. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics 47: 1-26. DOI 10.5774/47-0-213.
sources.note: Sec. 3 'Phonological overview' (vowels, consonants, syllable/morpheme structure, tone). Sec. 3.4 Tone, p. 11: 'all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system' (quoting Alex 1989:24), L and H plus downstep, tone anchored on vowels and syllabic nasals; Odual minimal tone pairs from Kari 2009: 9, 12 (ózú 'to pour' / òzú 'skin'); tone distinguishes statement vs question in Odual (Kari 2009:12). No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the 26 pages.

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 2 gives the 20-vowel system (10 single + 10 double vowels, ATR harmony; double vowels = one syllable of two moras) and fn. 5 (p. 94) states 'two basic tones in Odual, low and high, plus a downstep'; tone patterns of every pronoun are described. Data from the Adibaam dialect; Comson 1987 named as the detailed phonology.

The high tone is marked ( '), while the downstep is marked (6·6) with an arrow pointing downwards between two high-toned moras. In general, the low tone is not marked for the sake of convenience. … Tonally, the first person singular and first person plural exclusive subject pronouns have a high tone pattern, i.e. all moras are high toned; … while the second person singular subject pronoun has a high-downstepped-high tone pattern.

tone.says: Two level tones, low and high, plus a downstepped high between two highs; tones are assigned mora by mora (a long vowel is one syllable of two moras); tone also marks grammatical distinctions.

sources.quote: Tone is another interesting phonological characteristic of Rivers State languages. In all Rivers State languages, the pitch of the voice can be used to distinguish words, phrases and sentences whose segmental compositions are otherwise the same. [...] The tones that are attested in Rivers State languages include high (́), mid (ˉ), low (̀), and downstepped-high tone (a phonetically lowered high tone in the environment of a preceding floating low tone represented with an arrow pointing downwards between two high-toned syllables σ́ꜜσ́).
sources.locator: p. 11, sec. 5.1 Phonological Profile of Rivers State Languages
sources.note: Sec. 5.1 'Phonological Profile of Rivers State Languages', p. 11: in all Rivers State languages (Odual included) pitch distinguishes words, phrases and sentences (lexical and grammatical tone); tones attested across the state are H, M, L and downstepped H (downstep = H lowered after a floating L). Low tone left unmarked in the data (fn., p. 10). No Odual-specific tone inventory is given; for that the paper defers to Kari 2009 (ch. 1.3 Tone, pp. 11-12: lexical and grammatical tone) and Kari 2007 fn. 5 (two tones L, H plus downstep).
sources.venue: Marang: Journal of Language and Literature
